stem: (Select TWO.) Corriedale Metals runs some servers on-premises and some in the cloud, and wants to add both kinds of infrastructure using one configuration language and one applied workflow, rather than a separate native tool for each environment. Which two approaches meet this goal?

choices.text: Use the cloud vendor's own native provisioning tool for the cloud servers, and a separate on-premises automation tool for the on-premises servers.

Provision the cloud servers with the cloud vendor's own native tool, and configure the on-premises servers with a configuration-management tool that only manages settings on machines that already physically exist.
Declare an on-premises provider alongside a cloud provider in the same configuration, and apply both through the same plan-and-apply sequence.
Export the cloud configuration as a template and hand it to the on-premises team to reimplement in their own tool.
Rely on the provider model so the same core engine calls whichever plugin is appropriate to the platform, cloud or on-premises, that a given resource block targets.

rationale: Declaring an on-premises provider next to a cloud provider in one configuration, applied through one workflow, is the direct mechanism for a hybrid setup. That mechanism works because the same core engine simply calls whichever plugin matches a given resource block's platform. Using the cloud vendor's native tool plus a separate on-premises tool is exactly the two-toolchain outcome they want to avoid. A configuration-management tool only configures on-premises machines that already exist; it does not provision them in the first place, and it is still a second, separate tool from the cloud vendor's own. Exporting a template for the on-premises team to reimplement in their own tool still ends up as two separate representations, not one configuration language.
